title: Learning from Noisy Preferences: Semi-Supervised Direct Preference Optimization
one_liner: Filter messy human preference labels into clean and noisy subsets, train on clean data first, then use that model to give honest labels to the noisy data.
lead: When humans rate image pairs, they judge many things at once: does it look good, does it have fine detail, does it match what you asked for. But existing preference datasets just say winner or loser. A single image might be prettier but blurry, while another is detailed but ugly, yet one is marked as winner anyway. This creates conflicting signals that pull the model in opposite directions. Semi-DPO untangles this by first finding agreement on clean labels, training on those, then using that trained model to fix the noisy labels.

problem.h2: Messy human preference labels pull the model in conflicting directions
paras: A diffusion model (a neural network that generates images by starting with noise and learning to remove it) gets better when trained on human preferences. A human rates pairs of generated images, marking which is better, because the model learns to imitate the patterns that humans prefer. But humans judge many dimensions at once: whether the image looks realistic, has sharp details, follows the prompt, or feels aesthetically pleasing.

When a dataset compresses all those dimensions into a single winner-or-loser label, the result is noise. One image is prettier but missing details. Another is detailed but slightly off-topic. Yet one gets marked winner and the other loser, even though the preference is genuinely mixed. The model trained on such labels gets conflicting nudges: make prettier images here, make detailed images there. These contradictions slow learning and trap the model away from good solutions.

callout.html: Semi-DPO splits preference labels into clear agreement and conflicting ones, trains clean on agreement first, then auto-fixes the conflicting labels using the trained model.

steps.text: For each image pair, compute how much the human ratings align on all quality dimensions.
Mark pairs with clear agreement as clean; pairs with conflicting signals as noisy.
Run standard preference training on the clean subset only; model learns from honest signals.
The trained model now scores the noisy image pairs; these model-assigned labels replace human noise.
Retrain the model on both clean and newly-labeled noisy data; repeat until stable.

paras: The paper replaces the raw human preference labels with a two-stage labeling scheme: clean consensus labels first, then model-generated labels for noisy pairs. This changes the actual training data the diffusion model learns from.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: label agreement across dimensions
hidden.name: preference consensus
paras: Preference consensus is how much human raters agree that one image is better than the other across all the quality dimensions they evaluate. If all judges say image A is prettier, more detailed, and on-topic, the consensus is high, because all raters are pointing the model in the same direction. If some say A is prettier but others prefer B's details, the consensus is low, because different raters want contradictory things.

Semi-DPO measures consensus by checking whether the same pair gets consistent rank ordering across all quality aspects. The paper uses this to split the dataset: high consensus pairs become the clean training set, low consensus pairs become noisy ones to be relabeled by the model.

heat.caption: Darker means high agreement across all dimensions; lighter means conflicting ratings.

reads.html: Look at an image pair and ask: do all the humans who rate it agree it is better in every way? If yes, the pair has high consensus, because training on it will push the model in one clear direction. If humans split (one says prettier, one says less detailed), consensus is low, because different training signals pull the model apart.

Semi-DPO uses multi-dimensional preference ratings (lists of numbers, one score per quality dimension) to compute a consensus score per pair. Pairs above a threshold go into the clean set; those below go into noisy. The model is trained on clean first, then assigns new labels to the noisy set.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: two-stage training breaks the conflicting-signal trap
paras: Conflicting labels create a training trap: the model pulls toward contradictory targets, unable to settle. The first move is to train only on pairs where humans genuinely agree. The model then learns a coherent understanding of good images without the noise.

In the second stage, this trained model acts as a judge. When it looks at a noisy pair (one that humans disagreed on), it assigns a label based on its learned understanding. These model-generated labels are more honest than the original messy human ones, because they come from a model that learned only from clean agreement. When the model retrains on both clean and newly-labeled noisy pairs, it reinforces what it learned but now on a larger dataset.

The reason this works mechanically: a model trained on honest signals learns a stable direction of improvement. When it then labels the conflicting pairs, those labels point in the same direction, breaking the tug-of-war. The model can now move forward instead of oscillating.

stages.s: All preference pairs with multi-dimensional human ratings
Use model to label low-agreement pairs
Retrain on both clean and auto-labeled
Diffusion model aligned with multi-dimensional preferences

math.h2: The core idea as an equation
math.words: loss equals the preference ranking loss on the clean pairs plus a regularization term that pulls the model's labels on noisy pairs toward confidence in its own predictions
symbols: ranking loss on the high-agreement subset; theta is the model weights
loss on noisy pairs with model-generated labels y_model
how much to weight the noisy-pair learning relative to clean learning
the labels the trained model assigns to the low-agreement pairs

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the clean subset has loss 0.15 and the noisy subset has model-loss 0.22.
Set lambda = 0.8 (rely more on clean learning, less on noisy).
If lambda = 0.1 (ignore noisy), total = 0.15 + 0.01 = 0.16 (less learning from data).
If lambda = 2.0 (over-trust noisy), total = 0.15 + 0.44 = 0.59 (model might revert to old errors).
The sweet spot balances learning new data without undoing what the model learned from clean pairs.

math.note: The clean loss shapes the core learning; the pseudo-labeled loss extends it gently. Lambda controls how much to trust the model's own labels on disagreement.

charts.title: Without Semi-DPO
charts.note: Training on mixed labels creates low alignment across all dimensions because conflicting signals prevent learning any one direction well.

charts.title: With Semi-DPO
charts.note: Two-stage training on clean then auto-labeled data lets the model align with all dimensions simultaneously because the signals now point the same way.

items.html: If the consensus threshold is set too high, almost all pairs are marked noisy, leaving a tiny clean set. The model trains on too little data and learns slowly. If the threshold is too low, too many conflicting pairs sneak into clean, and the first training round fails to learn a coherent direction.

items.b: Model overfits its own mistakes early.
items.html: If the model trained on clean data has a blind spot (e.g. always generates ugly colors), it will stamp that same mistake onto the noisy labels. Then retraining reinforces the error instead of fixing it.

If lambda is too high, the model over-trusts its own noisy labels and forgets what it learned from clean data. If lambda is too low, the pseudo-labels barely contribute and most of the noisy data is wasted.

Set consensus threshold by inspection of the data. Train the clean model until it stabilizes. Use a moderate lambda so the second stage extends, not overrides, the first. Validate the model's pseudo-labels against a held-out human-labeled set to catch early overfitting.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple diffusion model (or use a toy image generator) and a dataset of 200 image pairs, each rated on two dimensions (e.g. realism and detail). Inject noise into 100 of the pairs by flipping one dimension's rating. Run standard preference learning on all 200 pairs, and measure alignment with each dimension. Then run Semi-DPO: filter the clean 100 pairs, train the model on clean, use it to relabel the noisy 100, retrain on all 200. Compare the two models' learned preferences.
demo.closing: The demo must show that Semi-DPO's two-stage labeling produces a model that aligns better with all dimensions at once, because training first on clean agreement then extending with auto-corrected noisy data lets the model stabilize in a direction that satisfies all dimensions, while the single-stage model gets pulled in conflicting directions and aligns with none because it never escapes the tug-of-war.
